title: Why Persuasion Is A Poor Classroom Management Strategy gement-strategy/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the widespread practice of pulling students aside to try to talk, reason, or plead them into behaving, arguing it is an exercise in futility that makes behavior worse. He identifies five specific harms: it wastes instructional time, it's stressful for both parties, it often escalates into arguments, it pushes students away by putting them on the defensive, and it lets them off the hook by substituting a talking-to for real accountability. He contrasts persuasion with genuine influence, which comes from students being naturally drawn to a teacher rather than pressured by one, and urges readers to abandon private powwows in favor of building likability, humor, and rapport, letting the classroom management plan itself do the persuading.
points: Attempting to persuade misbehaving students through private talks is described as time-consuming, stressful, and ultimately counterproductive.
Persuasion conversations frequently escalate into reprimands, threats, or arguments that damage the student-teacher relationship.
Pulling students aside to talk about behavior lets them off the hook, substituting a conversation for genuine accountability.
Real influence comes from students being drawn to a teacher through likability and rapport, not from pressure or persuasion tactics.
Teachers are urged to abandon private powwows and instead let a well-taught classroom management plan do the work of shaping behavior.
quotes: But the truth is, trying to persuade students to behave is an exercise in futility that causes behavior to get worse, not better.
Pulling students aside for private talks takes you away from what you should be doing, that is teaching, observing, and managing your class.

Meeting with individual students about their behavior will weaken your influence with them. It causes them to instinctively put up their guard, pull back from you and into a protective shell, and see you in a unfavorable light.
Trying to persuade students to behave absolves them of responsibility. They know that if they endure your talking-to, they’re free to go without further consequence.
Influence comes from students being drawn to you. It’s not something that can be extracted from them.
Tap into your likability, your humor, and your rapport with your students. Become a leader they respect and look up to. And leave the persuading to your classroom management plan.
